en: The Jātaka: The Section of Eighty [Birth Stories],
Chapter on the Lesser Swan (Cūḷahaṃsavagga)
2. The Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka:
“These swans are flying away, their bodies trembling with fear.”
O Haritaca, golden-hued one,
O Sumukha, depart as you wish;
leaving me behind, the host of kinsmen—
One has fallen under the power of the snare;
others go on without looking back—
why do you alone remain behind?
Of those who fall, the winged are best;
there is no companionship for the bound.
Do not let yourself be lost to that which is free from distress.
"By all means, Sumukha, go forth.
"Even if I were overcome by suffering,
O Dhatarattha, I would not abandon you."
Whether life or death shall be mine,
it will be together with you; even though overcome by suffering,
I [shall not go elsewhere].
O Dhatarattha, leave me alone;
you ought not to involve me in actions associated with the ignoble.
I am your friend, Sakumāra,
and I abide within your heart;
I am known to you as Senāpati.
O supreme among swans!
Having gone from here into the midst of my kinsmen, how shall I boast?
"O best of those who fly, having abandoned that [world],
what shall I say to you now that you have departed?
Here I shall give up my life."
“I do not dare to act ignobly.
“For this, Sumukha, is the Dhamma:
that you stand firm upon the path of the noble ones;”
He who, though I am his master and his friend,
does not wish to abandon me— while I am looking upon him, [I see] that very person...
No fear arises at all;
you shall attain such a life from me as this.”
While the noble ones, who live the lives of the noble, were thus conversing,
a hunter took up his staff.
Āpatī rushed forward with great force.
Seeing him rushing toward him,
Sumukha spoke these words in response:
The swan stood before the king, dispelling his fear with confidence:
"Do not fear, O best of those who fly; I shall carry you."
For such as these do not fear;
I shall apply myself to the practice that is appropriate and endowed with the Dhamma.
"By this means,
you will quickly be released from the snare.
Having heard those words of his,
At the well-spoken words of Sumukha,
the hunter, his hair standing on end with joy,
bowed with palms joined in reverence.
“Never have I heard or seen,
O bird among men, that the noble Vakkaṅga, speaking as one who is truly noble, should say such a thing.”
Abandoning his human voice:
"How indeed can he be a brahmin?
You, being yourself free, pay homage to one who is bound."
"The birds are departing;
why are you left behind alone?
"He is my king, O friend of the twice-born."
I had a palace built for the commander-in-chief;
yet I was unable to surrender that lord of birds to him at his request.
My husband belongs to a great company;
let him not meet with misfortune alone.
Thus, O hunter, do you lead him safely.
“I delight in you, O Lord.
“You follow the noble way, Vakkaṅga,
you who honor the alms-food.”
“I release you from that husband;
both of you may go as you please. “If, by my own effort, ...
[the verse continues] ...”
"O you who possess the wings of a swan,
we accept this gift of fearlessness from you, my friend."
It was not through our own effort that we were placed among the swans;
being powerless, let us go free.
“O hunter, you would commit theft!
Since you are a servant of that king,
do as you wish for him alone!”
"In this matter, King Saṃyama will act according to his understanding.
Thus spoke the hunter.
Golden-hued and green-skinned,
he grasped both hands and placed him inside a cage.
Those two birds, of radiant hue,
having entered the cage—
Sumukha and Dhataraṭṭha—
The hunter took him and departed.
As he was being carried away, Dhataraṭṭha said this to Sumukha:
“I am greatly afraid, O fair-faced one,
of Sāmā with the well-proportioned thighs;
she intends our slaughter.”
Then he will destroy himself.
And there are the pākahaṁsa, the sumukha,
the suhema, and the hemasuttacā.
“Like a heron on the shore of the ocean,
she surely appears miserable.
“So great is this world...”
Immeasurable and possessing a great following,
one should grieve for this alone,
and not as those possessed of wisdom do.
As the wind carries away both good and bad odors,
so the fool [seizes] both the raw and the cooked.
Like a blind man reaching for meat, you,
dull-witted and ignorant of the meaning of things,
have spoken to me with feeble wit.
"You do not know what should and should not be done;
you have reached the end of your time.
Intoxicated with pride, you have uttered [this]."
Those who consider women to be superior—
these are common to many,
like a tavern to drunkards.
This is illusion and a mirage,
sorrow, disease, and calamity;
these are harsh and bonds.
The snares of death dwell within these caves;
the person who places his trust in them is the lowest of men among men.”
Who is worthy to censure that which was ordained by the elders?
They are indeed called the women of great supernatural power.
They appeared in the world.
Play was directed toward them,
and delight was established in them.
Seeds grow within them—
namely, beings who are born there—
who would not feel revulsion for them?
Having laid hold of one another with their hands,
you alone, O fair-faced one, and no other,
employ women in matters of wealth.
When fear has arisen for you today,
a mind born of terror takes birth;
for everyone who has fallen into doubt, [this happens].
The wise and great ones endure fear; they apply themselves to what is meaningful,
even when it is difficult to practice.
It is for this purpose that kings desire a wise hero—
one who wards off what the hero would otherwise oppose.
This is my own personal misfortune.
Let not the king’s cooks in the great kitchen harm us today.
For indeed, the color of the fallen leaves was like the fruit of the bamboo;
even though he was released, he did not wish to fly up.
He has come upon his own bondage;
having fallen into doubt today,
grasp the meaning, not the mere words.
Therefore, apply yourself to that practice which is appropriate and endowed with the Dhamma; through your diligent application,
[you shall attain the goal].
“Seek alms for me. “Do not fear, O best of those who fall;
for such as you do not fear.”
I shall apply myself to the practice,
which is appropriate and connected with the Dhamma;
by means of my diligent application, [may I attain it].
"you will quickly be released from the snare.
Then that hunter, carrying the swan-skin,
approached the king's gate.
“Announce me to the king, saying:
‘Dhataraṭṭha has arrived.
Having seen them, those who were the manifesters of merit—
To those two who were recognized for their auspicious marks,
King Saṃyama addressed his ministers.
“Give garments to the hunter,
as well as food, drink, and sustenance;
let there be as much gold as he desires.”
"However many he desires.
Having seen the hunter's state of serene confidence,
the King of Kāsi then said:
“If this, friend Khemaka,
stands amidst full-blown lotuses,
how has it come to find delight therein?”
Approaching with a noose in his hand,
he took up the conversation, which was crowded by the assembly of kinsmen and devoid of moderation.
“Today is the seventh night for me,
subsisting on alms;
seeking this state, I have not yet found it.”
Diligent and striving,
I then beheld his track as he moved about, free from seeking.
There I set a snare;
thus I caught that bird.
"Hunter, these two birds—"
Now you say you are alone;
is your mind indeed perverted,
or what do you wish to conquer?
“For one whose red palms shine like refined gold and are beautiful,
standing with chest held firm— ”
He came to my place of confinement.
Then this radiant bird, though unbound,
[approached] me who was bound and distressed.
He stood there proclaiming himself noble,
abandoning his human speech.
"Then what now, O Sumukha?"
"You stand here with your jaw clenched;
you have come before my assembly,
yet out of fear you do not speak."
“O Lord of Kāsi, it is not out of fear that I have entered your assembly;
it is not out of fear that I shall not speak.”
“Your speech regarding such a matter [is as follows]:
‘I see no reinforcements for you—
neither chariots nor foot soldiers.’”
Neither his hide nor his insect,
nor the armored archer;
neither silver nor gold.
Or a well-constructed city,
with its moats filled, difficult to assault,
and possessing strong watchtowers and ramparts.
“Where you have entered, O Sumukha,
you do not fear what should be feared.
“I have no need for pursuers;”
Neither by city nor by wealth;
we travel along paths that are no paths,
for we are wanderers through the sky.
We are learned and wise,
skillful thinkers on what is meaningful;
let us speak words endowed with meaning.
He is established in truth.
What can you do, being untruthful and ignoble?
Even well-spoken words from a liar and a cruel man—
those [words] are accepted because of the authority of the brahmins.
He has established this security;
and this freedom from fear has been proclaimed by you throughout these ten directions.
Having plunged into that lotus pond,
pure with its serene waters,
where there was an abundance of food, they ate their fill.
"And non-violence toward birds.
Having heard this proclamation,
we have come into your presence.
Bound by that very noose of yours,
this speech of yours is false. Having placed false speech at the forefront, [you have spoken thus].
And evil desire and greed—
having transcended both these bonds,
one is reborn into a state of suffering.
“We did not neglect you, Sumukha,
nor did we follow the path out of greed;
for we have heard the wise on this matter.”
Skilled thinkers of meaning,
having come here, might speak even words that possess little substance.
“O hunter, you have spoken thus to me with a pleasant face; therefore,
O Lord of Kāsi, do not be afraid.”
Since life has been brought to its end,
speak words that possess meaning,
for the time of death has arrived.
He who kills a deer with a deer,
or a bird with a bird,
or buys a learned man with what he has heard—
What is more ignoble than this:
one who utters the speech of the noble while being steeped in ignoble qualities?
He falls away from both worlds,
both here and in the world beyond.
Having attained fame, one should not become intoxicated.
One should not entertain doubt regarding one's illness;
rather, one should strive in one's duties and close up all vulnerabilities.
Those who have grown old and passed beyond,
having reached the appointed time,
and having practiced the Dhamma here—
Thus they have gone to the third heaven.
Having heard this, O Lord of Kāsi,
protect the Dhamma within yourself.
"Release Dhataraṭṭha, the most excellent among swans.
"Let them bring water for washing the feet," [he said].
And his costly throne;
I shall release the illustrious Dhataraṭṭha from his cage.
And that general who is wise,
skillful, and a thinker of the king's welfare,
who shares in the king's happiness when he is happy—
When others are suffering, he too suffers.
Such a person indeed deserves to eat the alms-food of the donor.
"Just as this Sumukha is the king’s dear friend, sharing his very life;
and the throne made entirely of gold,"
Dhataraṭṭha entered [the hall], which was eight-footed, delightful, polished,
and spread with Kāsī cloth.
And Sumukha entered [the palace], which had a couch made entirely of gold and draped with a tiger-skin coverlet.
Immediately after Dhatarattha,
the Kasi people, having taken many golden bowls, [offered them].
They brought offerings to the swans,
presented by the supreme king;
having seen that supreme gift brought to them, they—
It was sent by the King of Kāsi;
skilled in the duties of a kshatriya,
he then questioned him immediately thereafter.
“Is it well with you, sir? Are you free from illness?
Is this kingdom prosperous?”
"You instruct us according to the Dhamma.
"It is indeed wholesome for me, O swan,
and moreover, it is free from affliction, O swan."
"And so, may I righteously govern this prosperous kingdom.
"I trust that among your ministers..."
No fault whatsoever is found in you;
and do they not desire your life for the sake of their own welfare?
“Furthermore, no fault whatsoever exists among my ministers;
yet they [act] against my interests.”
They do not long for life.
“Is your wife like you—
obedient and sweet-spoken?”
“Endowed with sons, beauty, and fame,
she follows your will and pleasure.
Moreover, my wife is her equal.”
Obedient and sweet-spoken;
endowed with the beauty and fame of a son,
she follows my will and authority.
“I hope the kingdom is free from oppression,
with no calamities from any quarter,
and governed by non-violent righteousness?”
“You instruct with impartiality.
Furthermore, the kingdom is free from oppression and has no calamities from any quarter.
“Teaching by means of non-violence and through the Dhamma with impartiality.
“Are the virtuous honored?”
The wicked have been avoided;
if you do not reject the Dhamma,
you will follow what is contrary to the Dhamma.
The virtuous are honored by me,
and the unvirtuous are avoided;
I follow only the Dhamma.
“Unrighteousness has been cast out by me.
“I trust you, O Kṣatriya, do not overlook the long duration of the future?”
“Am I intoxicated by intoxicants,
so that I do not fear the world beyond?
“I am not afraid of the long future;”
I contemplate this, O bird;
established in the ten qualities,
I do not fear the world beyond.
Generosity, virtue, renunciation,
uprightness, gentleness,
austerity, non-anger, and non-harming—
Patience and non-opposition—
thus I see these wholesome states established within myself.
From that, rapture arises within me,
and no small measure of gladness;
and Sumukha, without reflecting, [spoke].
This bird of ours, failing to understand the corruption of his own mind, uttered harsh words.
Thus, being angry, you uttered harsh words in an improper manner;
such things are not found among us.
"This is not like those who possess wisdom.
"I have this dysentery, O lord of men;
it has come upon me with great force."
When Dhatarattha was bound,
great suffering came upon me.
You are like a father to us, his children.
Like the earth that supports all beings,
may you, O elephant among kings,
forgive us who have transgressed against you.
“We rejoice in this of yours,
that you do not conceal your true nature;
you shatter the barrenness within, O bird.”
You are upright, O bird.
Whatever treasure there is in the residence of the King of Kāsi, [all that is yours].
Silver and gold,
pearls and many beryl gems,
jewels, conch shells, and pearls.
Cloth, yellow sandalwood;
antelope skins, ivory articles,
and much iron and black metal.
“I give this wealth to you;
I relinquish my sovereignty to you.
“Surely we have been honored by you,” they said.
And you are honored, O bull among charioteers;
for those who abide in the teachings,
please be our teacher.
O Teacher, we are approved by you; having been authorized by you,
we shall pay homage to you by keeping you to our right.
“May we see our kinsman, O Subduer of Enemies.
Having reflected throughout the entire night and deliberated according to the truth, they spoke.
The King of Kāśī gave permission to the most excellent of swans; then,
at the end of the night,
As the Kasi king watched the rising of the sun,
those [rays] entered his palace.
When those supreme brahmins had arrived safely and were seen,
the swans cried out, "Where are they? and made a great outcry.
A great sound arose.
Delighted by their husband who had been released,
they, out of reverence for their husband, [shouted].
Birds that had found their opportunity gathered all around;
such are the benefits for those who possess friends.
All were auspicious;
like swans of Dhatarattha,
they approached the assembly of kinsmen.
The Second Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka.
